GPU

Source: vignettes/gpu.Rmd
gpu.Rmd

By default, all models run on the CPU. A GPU can speed up very large analyses, but it is not always faster than the CPU. How fast it is depends on batch_size and n_workers, so try a few values on a sample of your data before a large run (see Workers and batch size).

Platform GPU Setup
Linux NVIDIA birdnet_use_gpu("pt") or birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
Linux AMD (experimental) UV_TORCH_BACKEND, then birdnet_use_gpu("pt")
macOS, Apple silicon built-in birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
Windows NVIDIA your own Python environment
any NVIDIA, with ONNX Runtime your own Python environment

Backends

Not every backend can use a GPU:

  • "pt" (PyTorch, BirdNET+ V3.0 only) and "pb" (TensorFlow, all models including Perch v2) can.
  • "onnx" can, but only in a Python environment you set up yourself (see ONNX Runtime).
  • "tf" (TensorFlow Lite) runs on the CPU only.

birdnet_use_gpu() adds the Python packages needed for GPU support. Call it at the top of your script, before you load any model, because the packages are installed when Python starts. Choose one backend per R session: TensorFlow and PyTorch each bring their own CUDA libraries, which can conflict. To switch, restart R.

Then pass device = "GPU" when you predict or encode. If something does not work, restart R without birdnet_use_gpu() to go back to the CPU.

The GPU packages are large downloads; see Download progress.

Workers and batch size

Two arguments of birdnet_predict() and birdnet_encode() decide how well the GPU is used:

  • n_workers: each worker is a separate process with its own copy of the model on the GPU. With device = "GPU", birdnetR starts one worker per GPU unless you set n_workers. More workers can keep a large GPU busier, but each one needs its own GPU memory and RAM.
  • batch_size: how many segments the GPU processes at once. The default of 1 leaves most of a GPU idle. Larger values such as 32L or 64L are usually faster and need more GPU memory.
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU", batch_size = 32L)

Larger batches work with the PyTorch ("pt") and ONNX Runtime ("onnx") backends, with BirdNET V2.4 and with Perch v2. The BirdNET+ V3.0 model on the TensorFlow backend ("pb") only accepts batch_size = 1. Tune n_workers there and skip the batch_size steps below.

The best values depend on your GPU, so time a sample of your data (for example 30 minutes of audio):

  1. Start with one worker (the default) and batch_size = 32L.
  2. Double batch_size until it stops getting faster or the GPU runs out of memory.
  3. Try n_workers = 2L. Keep it only if it is clearly faster, because every worker puts another copy of the model into GPU memory and RAM.
  4. Run the same sample on the CPU (without device = "GPU") and compare.

On AMD GPUs, time the second run of each setting: the first run with a new batch_size includes compiling GPU code (see ROCm).

If memory runs out, see High memory or CPU use.

Linux with an NVIDIA GPU: PyTorch 

birdnet_use_gpu("pt")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pt")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

This installs birdnet[pt]. If the environment variable UV_TORCH_BACKEND is not set, birdnetR sets it to "auto", so the installer picks the PyTorch build that matches your GPU driver. The NVIDIA driver must be installed.

To check that PyTorch can see your GPU (NVIDIA or AMD), run this after loading the model:

reticulate::import("torch")$cuda$is_available()
#> [1] TRUE

Linux with an NVIDIA GPU: TensorFlow 

birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pb")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

# Perch v2
perch <- birdnet_load_perch(device = "GPU")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(perch, files, device = "GPU")

This installs birdnet[and-cuda], TensorFlow with its CUDA libraries. The NVIDIA driver and CUDA must already be installed on your system.

To check that TensorFlow can see your GPU, run this after loading the model:

reticulate::import("tensorflow")$config$list_physical_devices("GPU")
#> [[1]]
#> PhysicalDevice(name='/physical_device:GPU:0', device_type='GPU')

An empty list means TensorFlow runs on the CPU. TensorFlow 2.21.0 does this even when everything is installed, because it does not find one of the CUDA libraries. birdnet_use_gpu("pb") leaves that version out; if you manage your own Python environment, install another TensorFlow version there.

Linux with an AMD GPU (ROCm, experimental)

PyTorch has builds for AMD GPUs (ROCm). Tell the installer which one to use before calling birdnet_use_gpu():

Sys.setenv(UV_TORCH_BACKEND = "rocm7.2")
birdnet_use_gpu("pt")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pt")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

The value names a PyTorch build, and uv accepts only the builds it knows. If you give another value, uv stops with an error that lists the valid ones. Use the newest rocmX.Y from that list; older values can pull in an older PyTorch release. PyTorch’s ROCm builds include the ROCm libraries they need, so the value does not have to match a ROCm version installed on your system.

The ROCm build of PyTorch is about 6 GB to download. The first run with a new batch_size can take a minute or two while ROCm compiles its GPU code; later runs reuse it.

ROCm support is experimental: not every AMD GPU is supported by ROCm. Check that PyTorch can see your GPU as shown above. Integrated GPUs share memory with the CPU and may not be faster than it (see Workers and batch size).

macOS with Apple silicon: TensorFlow with Metal 

birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pb")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

This installs birdnet[tf] and tensorflow-metal, Apple’s GPU plugin for TensorFlow. Two caveats:

  • The birdnet Python package lists GPU use of the Protobuf ("pb") backend on macOS as unsupported.
  • tensorflow-metal often lags behind TensorFlow releases, so the newest TensorFlow may not work with it yet.

The BirdNET+ V3.0 release on Zenodo also has Core ML files (.mlpackage) for iOS and macOS apps. The birdnet Python package can’t use Core ML yet, so birdnetR can’t either (see birdnet#101).

ONNX Runtime: bring your own environment

The GPU version of ONNX Runtime (onnxruntime-gpu) has to replace the regular onnxruntime, which the birdnet package depends on. birdnetR can’t do that in its managed environment, so you create your own environment once. You need an NVIDIA GPU with the CUDA and cuDNN versions that ONNX Runtime requires.

# Once: create a virtual environment with birdnet and onnxruntime-gpu.
# It needs Python 3.11 to 3.13 on your system (see reticulate::install_python()).
reticulate::virtualenv_create("birdnet-gpu", version = "3.12")
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "birdnet>=1.5,<2")
reticulate::virtualenv_remove("birdnet-gpu", packages = "onnxruntime", confirm = FALSE)
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "onnxruntime-gpu")

In every session, point RETICULATE_PYTHON at this environment before you load the first model (or set it in your .Renviron file):

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = reticulate::virtualenv_python("birdnet-gpu"))
library(birdnetR)

model <- birdnet_load()
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

If you later upgrade birdnet in this environment, check whether onnxruntime has come back, and remove it again if so. Extras such as TensorFlow are not installed automatically in your own environment (see Your own Python environment).

Windows

On Windows, birdnet_use_gpu() stops with an error because there is no automatic setup. Set up your own Python environment once, as for ONNX Runtime. You need an NVIDIA GPU and its driver.

For PyTorch, install a CUDA build of PyTorch first, then birdnet:

# Once:
reticulate::virtualenv_create("birdnet-gpu", version = "3.12")
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "torch",
  pip_options = "--index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128"
)
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "birdnet[pt]>=1.5,<2")

Take the cuXYZ value that fits your driver from the PyTorch installation page. Then, in every session:

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = reticulate::virtualenv_python("birdnet-gpu"))
library(birdnetR)

model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pt")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

For ONNX Runtime, follow the ONNX Runtime section above; it works the same way on Windows.

TensorFlow ("pb") does not support GPUs on native Windows. If you run R in WSL2 (the Windows Subsystem for Linux), follow the Linux sections instead.
